title: DWCZ – CO – Betasso Meteorological Tower — 2020–2026 (DWCZ-BT-Met)
display_name: DWCZ – CO – Betasso Meteorological Tower — 2020–2026 (DWCZ-BT-Met)
abstract: The Betasso 10 m Meteorological Tower is part of the Dynamic Water Critical Zone (DWCZ) network and provides continuous atmospheric, radiation, and soil observations for the Betasso catchment near Boulder, Colorado. The station records wind speed, wind direction, air temperature, and relative humidity at 10 m; incoming shortwave radiation at 5 m; and net radiation at 1.6 m. A tipping-bucket rain gage is mounted near 1 m, and soil temperature and moisture probes are installed at approximately 20 cm below the surface. All instruments are wired to a Campbell Scientific CR1000 (s/n 16759) datalogger. Data are collected to support long-term monitoring of meteorological conditions and energy–water fluxes across the DWCZ network. Sensor coordinates, elevations, and calibration details are provided in the accompanying metadata files. DATASET STATUS NOTE **Dataset Status:** Concluded (Inactive) The formal project officially ended on **August 30, 2024**. However, station infrastructure and active data downloads for the Bettasso Met Tower (BT_MET) systems were maintained post-project until **August 9, 2026**. Data collection ceased on this date due to unknown reasons. While the physical array remains deployed on-site, no data has been logged past August 9, 2026. Legacy data are archived here: https://www.hydroshare.org/resource/6bf3e44b9de344749d8f665e139e7311/

title: Data from: Moving beyond Bergmann and Converse Bergmann: Can competition or food resources drive spatial variation in body size?
display_name: Data from: Moving beyond Bergmann and Converse Bergmann: Can competition or food resources drive spatial variation in body size?
abstract: Hypothesis testing for body size trends along elevational and latitudinal gradients is dominated by Bergmann’s rule predicting larger size in colder environments and Converse Bergmann’s rule predicting smaller size where summers are shorter. Despite the mixed to poor support for Bergmann’s and Converse Bergmann’s rules, alternative hypotheses are virtually untested along environmental gradients. Here we aim to contrast Bergmann’s and Converse Bergmann’s rules with alternative spatial hypotheses for intraspecific body size variation: intensity of competition and quantity of food resources across elevationally distributed sites. We use individuals from 11 species of carrion beetles (Staphylinidae: Silphinae) collected across 30 sites in two mountain ranges (Front Range and San Juan Mountains, Colorado, USA). We measure beetle body size (elytral length, estimated weight), quantify food availability, and estimate interference and exploitative competition from community abundance. Predictions of Bergmann’s rule and competition lacked support. Two of ten species supported Converse Bergmann’s rule. In contrast, within-site body size variation was significantly associated with local food abundance. Where food resources were abundant intraspecific body sizes spanned from very small to very large. Resource-poor sites yielded fewer, but uniform, average-sized individuals. Alternative aspects of life history can outweigh climate in shaping insect body size, thus potentially underlying inconsistent elevational body size patterns across studies.

title: Forest to Grass/Shrub transformation in the Western US from 2001-2012
display_name: Forest to Grass/Shrub transformation in the Western US from 2001-2012
abstract: This data release contains three raster layers that identify pixels of persistent forest-to-grass/shrub land cover change. The layers were derived from annual Land Change Monitoring, Assessment, and Projection (LCMAP) Land Cover Primary (LCPRI) rasters for 1985-2021. A pixel qualifies when (1) it is classified as Tree Cover (class 4) in the start year, 2001, and (2) at any point after 2001 it spends at least 10 consecutive years in Grass/Shrub (class 3). The qualifying run does not need to begin immediately after 2001 or to continue through 2021. The release includes a binary qualification layer, a layer giving the longest consecutive run (in years) spent in Grass/Shrub after 2001, and a layer giving the first year of the qualifying run. The rule was applied pixel by pixel using windowed, multithreaded processing in Python so that the full annual stack never has to be held in memory. To map areas where forest (Tree Cover) was converted to, and remained in, grass/shrub cover for a sustained period, for use in land cover change analysis we used before parameterization. Rule parameters: START_YEAR = 2001; PERSISTENCE_YEARS = 10; CLASS_FOREST = 4 (LCMAP Tree Cover); CLASS_GRASS = 3 (LCMAP Grass/Shrub). Because only years after 2001 are scanned for the run (2002-2021), the longest possible run is 20 years and a qualifying run can start no later than 2012. Land cover classes between the start year and the qualifying run are not restricted, so a pixel may pass through other classes before its grass/shrub run begins. An optional, stricter rule (REQUIRE_STABLE_BACK_TO_FIRST_YEAR = True) additionally requires Tree Cover in every year from 1985 through 2001; it was NOT used for the released layers unless stated otherwise by the author.

title: Lagomorph Inventory at Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve
display_name: Lagomorph Inventory at Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve
abstract: Rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus type 2 (RHDV2) has caused dramatic declines in rabbits and hares on several continents. Recent mortalities have been reported for several rabbit and hare species in the United States, suggesting broad susceptibility of lagomorphs. If this susceptibility extends to the American pika (Ochotona princeps), the most cold-adapted lagomorph, it could compound climate-mediated threats to this species. Due to climate change, American pikas are predicted to experience significant upslope range retraction during this century. To address this concern, we investigated spatial patterns of habitat use by pikas and other lagomorphs in Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve, which borders several counties that have reported RHDV2. In 2022, we surveyed 115 plots of pika habitats in the park, including 48 legacy plots from a pika survey conducted in 2010-2012. Our mean estimate of pika habitat occupancy was at least 95% during 2022 in GRSA, slightly higher than in 2010-2012. Leporid presence at these same plots was 48%. The best model of leporid presence supported a negative effect of elevation. Both models also included a positive effect of incoming solar radiation. Finally, we used our best models of pika habitat occupancy and leporid presence to map the potential for areas of contact and RHDV2 transmission between these taxa. Our results indicate some potential for contact within subalpine forests, specifically in the northern half of the park near the lower reach of the Sand Creek Trail and in the far south just north of California Peak. Citation: Peralta A and Ray C . Lagomorph Inventory at Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve. 2022. title: SNOW: Fast and Differentiable MHD Surrogate for Solar Wind using Neural Operator
display_name: SNOW: Fast and Differentiable MHD Surrogate for Solar Wind using Neural Operator
abstract: SNOW: Solar Neural Operator for Wind SNOW is an autoregressive neural operator trained to model the radial shell-to-shell evolution of eight MHD variables derived from AWSoM simulations. The model operates on a 91x180 angular grid and advances the solution by 10 solar wind per rollout step till 240 Rs (1.12 AU). The archived SNOW.pt file is the checkpoint used to generate the results reported in the SNOW manuscript.

title: An Inspectable LLM Council for Multi-Model Research Answer Aggregation: Evaluation Data and Reproduction Code
display_name: An Inspectable LLM Council for Multi-Model Research Answer Aggregation: Evaluation Data and Reproduction Code
abstract: This dataset and code package accompanies the manuscript "An Inspectable LLM Council for Multi-Model Research Answer Aggregation." It contains inputs for 100 DRACO tasks, 600 final model answers, 100 saved analyst states, and 720 whole-answer judgments, together with formal requests, retained raw responses, and derived analysis files. The Python analysis scripts reproduce the reported statistics, tables, and figures from the retained records without new API calls. ESM_1.zip preserves the original project-relative file paths. The README contains the reproduction commands and a guide to the archive contents. The authors' experiment records and derived artifacts are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Analysis code is licensed under the MIT License. DRACO-derived inputs and rubric material retain their MIT license and attribution to Perplexity AI, Inc., as specified in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md. title: Data and code from: Plant species responses to nutrient addition, but not to herbivore exclusion, strengthen over time in global grasslands
display_name: Data and code from: Plant species responses to nutrient addition, but not to herbivore exclusion, strengthen over time in global grasslands
abstract: Abstract Nutrient enrichment and altered herbivory are among the most pervasive drivers of change in grasslands worldwide, yet how their effects on plant communities accumulate or fade over time, and which species drive those effects, remains poorly resolved. Using long-term data from the Nutrient Network (NutNet), a globally distributed experiment, we examined how grassland plant community composition responded to factorial nutrient addition (NPK) and herbivore exclusion (fencing) across 98 sites and up to 12 years of treatment. For each site and year, we quantified the overall compositional difference between treatments (PERMANOVA), identified the species contributing most to those differences (SIMPER), and classified species as indicators of each treatment (Indicator Species Analysis), linking these responses to each species' dominance, commonness, functional group, lifespan, and provenance. We found that compositional divergence under nutrient addition strengthened over time and was driven disproportionately by a relatively small subset of species, particularly dominant and common ones, whereas the effects of herbivore exclusion were comparatively weak and transient. These results highlight the importance of species-level dynamics for understanding how grassland biodiversity responds to global change. This package provides the processed data and annotated R code needed to reproduce all analyses and figures in the associated study.

title: Structural Demand Consequences of Liquefaction and its Mitigation with Dense Granular Columns Using Machine Learning
display_name: Structural Demand Consequences of Liquefaction and its Mitigation with Dense Granular Columns Using Machine Learning
abstract: This research presents machine learning (ML)-based predictive models to predict critical engineering demand parameters (EDPs) for structures subject to liquefaction, specifically peak flexural story drifts (PSDR) and peak roof acceleration (PRA). Additionally, we include a metric to characterize the performance of the foundation, such as peak foundation accelerations (PFA). A comprehensive dataset consisting of approximately 4,000 three-dimensional, nonlinear, fully-coupled effective stress finite element analyses was created, validated with centrifuge experimental data, and designed using quasi-Monte Carlo sampling. The soil models consider realistic stratigraphically variable liquefiable deposits under both unmitigated and mitigated conditions with Dense Granular Columns (DGCs), applied to the center and periphery of the foundation. The project integrates advanced numerical simulations with ML models to improve prediction accuracy for structural and foundation response, key influencing factors, and mitigation design.

title: Accretion of Polydisperse and Heterogeneous Clouds
display_name: Accretion of Polydisperse and Heterogeneous Clouds
abstract: This dataset contains the simulation data used in support of the associated publication "Gravitational Accretion: the Deceptive Surfaces of Asteroids". It describes the time evolution of a collection of spherical particles stored in a single HDF5 file. For each sphere, the dataset provides its radius, position, and velocity. Positions and velocities are recorded for all saved time steps, while the radius is stored once for each particle as a time-independent quantity. The file is organized to facilitate direct reading and post-processing, with particle identifiers, time values, and kinematic variables stored in a structured and compact format. This dataset is intended to ensure reproducibility of the analyses and figures presented in the publication.

abstract: Particle-in-cell simulation data and analysis code supporting the paper "Nonlinear X-mode propagation in magnetized pair plasmas: dispersive shocks and sudden dissipation" by P. J. Bilbao, A. Wierzchucka, A. A. Schekochihin and D. A. Uzdensky. The paper studies finite-amplitude, low-frequency extraordinary modes (fast magnetosonic waves in the MHD limit) in a cold, strongly magnetized electron-positron plasma. Such waves steepen into a spatial cusp, are arrested by finite-frequency dispersion into a train of solitons, and above a threshold amplitude lose their energy abruptly when particles cross those solitons non-adiabatically. This archive contains the simulations behind every figure and every quoted number. Contents: 508 OSIRIS simulations, comprising all input decks, 413 energy histories, and the field and phase-space output used in the figures, together with the analysis code, the figure scripts and the figures themselves. The runs are grouped by campaign: amplitude scan (including the long run used to measure soliton widths and speeds), magnetization scan from σ = 2×10² to 10⁴, frequency scan, temperature scan at two pump frequencies, a moving-window run following a packet into a declining background field, and a tracked-particle run resolving individual soliton encounters. Conventions: lengths in c/ω_ce, times in 1/ω_ce, fields in units of B₀, and σ defined with the single-species plasma frequency. The reference scan uses σ = 1.6×10³ and ω₀ = 10⁻² ω_ce, with 500 macroparticles per cell per species. Exact parameters for any run are in its own input deck. README.md documents the layout, states which data produces which figure, and lists what was deliberately excluded: stdout logs, restart files, timing reports and raw per-rank track dumps, none of which carry scientific content. MANIFEST.csv lists every file with its size. Both are provided uncompressed next to the archive. The two-dimensional runs behind the transverse-stability figures of the supplement are deposited separately. Simulations were performed on MareNostrum 5 under EuroHPC-JU extreme scale access project EHPC-EXT-2025E02-066 (KEEP: Kinetic Electrodynamics in Extreme Plasmas). --- Arrangement: the deposit is split into one archive per campaign, together with xmode_00_code_and_figures.zip, which holds the analysis code, the figure scripts, the figures, the README and the manifest. Every archive stores the same top-level folder, so they line up: unzipping any subset into a single directory produces a consistent tree, and unzipping all of them reconstructs the complete deposit, in any order and with no renaming. A reader who needs only one campaign can therefore download that archive alone and still obtain a valid, self-describing subtree. To reassemble the whole deposit, put the archives in one directory and unzip them all, for example for z in xmode_*.zip; do unzip -q "$z"; done which yields a single folder, zenodo_xmode_dispersive_shocks/, laid out exactly as README.md describes. On Windows or macOS, selecting all the archives and extracting them to the same destination has the same effect; answer "merge" or "keep both" if asked, since no file occurs in more than one archive.

title: Full summary table for "The landscape of PGS prediction accuracy and transportability across the phenome in ancestrally diverse populations"
display_name: Full summary table for "The landscape of PGS prediction accuracy and transportability across the phenome in ancestrally diverse populations"
abstract: This folder contains summary data used by Lin et al. 2026 for all traits and all scores used in the manuscript. All files are tab delimited. The large "all_megatable_v2_w_header.txt.gz" file has 138 labeled columns, and it serves as the complete record of summary statistics and features for PGS by phecode associations. We also provide a dictionary file explaining column names and each column's data type, in "PGS_megatable_datadictionary.txt". Additionally, we provide line index of "all_megatable_v2_w_header.txt.gz" that can be used to extract the subset of the table used in HLMM analyses in the manuscript. These are 1-column files, 0-indexed, that give the rows used in each analysis (accounting for the header as line 0). These can be used to extract the rows that serve as input for the HLMMs.1. Significant set in continuous model, and an equal number of non-significant association pairs: "index_continuous_subset.txt.gz"2. Significant set in thresholded model, and an equal number of non-significant association pairs: "index_thresholded_subset.txt.gz" These should be intuitive and use standard labels, however don't hesitate to contact the authors should you have additional questions. (meng.lin@cuanschutz.edu) A web browser visualizing the top associations based on this summary table is available as Web Overview of Multi-ancestry Polygenic scores in Biobank Traits (WOMPBAT) at https://wompbat.simonwalker.tech/

display_name: ROMS with particle tracking configuration and simulations for the Kaktovik Lagoon chain, Alaska
abstract: This dataset includes output from a 50-186 m horizontal resolution, 5 vertical layer Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) simulation, with Lagrangian particle tracking, of the Kaktovik Lagoon chain along the Beaufort Sea coast of Alaska during the open water season from July 1 to September 30 of 2019. Included are three-hourly hydrodynamic output and hourly particle location. This output is made public in connection with a publication (Geller et al., 2026): Modeled variations in transport and export of riverine freshwater across a chain of Beaufort Sea lagoons for a range of open water season conditions. Also included are model input files and scripts necessary to rerun the model.
source_display_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Antarctic toothfish otolith reference set age data from the Ross Sea, Antarctica
display_name: Antarctic toothfish otolith reference set age data from the Ross Sea, Antarctica
abstract: Estimated ages for Antarctic toothfish using otoliths prepared via the bake, grind and polish method were validated and reported on by Brooks et al. 2011. The otoliths validated in the study by Brooks et al. 2011 serve as a reference set for all aging activities in the Brooks Lab and are permanently housed at the University of Colorado Boulder. The reference set collection was randomly sampled from a larger sample of 1,508 otoliths by Brooks et al. (2011). Estimated ages for the reference set collection for both viewing methods investigated (Monitor versus Direct) for the three readers in this study are defined in the dataset as HK, CG and RL. This study compared the precision and bias between the two viewing methods. The estimated ages established in the study by Brooks et al. 2011 by Reader 1 for the 185 otoliths selected for this study were compared with the consensus image view age estimates to serve as a between-method "proxy" comparison since both studies used the same otoliths. Reference set ages by Reader 1 in the Brooks et al. 2011 study are defined in the dataset as CB Direct R12. Note digits associated with each reader/method combination in each column header, for example HK Direct R14, represents the 14th time the reference set was aged by that ager. Individual readers may have required additional reads relative to other agers, however only the last two final reads of the reference set for each ager are reported on here as they served as the basis for comparison analyses.

title: Isotopic Evidence for Modification of Column Water Vapor by Cities: Code and Data
display_name: Isotopic Evidence for Modification of Column Water Vapor by Cities: Code and Data
abstract: This repository contains the code, data, and derived results supporting the manuscript “Isotopic Evidence for Modification of Column Water Vapor by Cities” by Martin Velez-Pardo, David C. Noone, and Richard P. Fiorella. The study investigates urban–rural differences in atmospheric water-vapor isotopic composition (δD) and total-column water vapor using TROPOMI satellite observations. A global analysis of large cities combines satellite-derived climatologies with settlement fraction, elevation, distance to major water bodies, and land-cover information to characterize seasonal urban–rural anomalies. An idealized two-layer isotope–moisture model is used to explore physically plausible mechanisms contributing to the observed patterns. The archive includes the Jupyter notebook implementing the analyses, the software environment, observational and ancillary datasets, processed city-season results, model outputs, figures, and supplementary sensitivity analyses. The directory structure preserves the relative paths used by the notebook, allowing the workflow to be reproduced after extraction. Reproducibility: Download and extract UrbanWaterVaporIsotopes_Zenodo.zip, follow the installation instructions in the included README, and execute UrbanWaterVaporIsotopes.ipynb from the project directory using the supplied environment.yml. Data sources and attribution: The accompanying DATA_SOURCES_AND_LICENSES.md file documents the original satellite and geographic data sources, dataset references, processing provenance, and applicable attribution and licensing terms. It should be consulted when using or redistributing materials from the archive. Software release and licensing: The original analysis software was approved for open-source release by Los Alamos National Laboratory under O5230. Copyright © 2026 Triad National Security, LLC. All rights reserved. The software is distributed under the BSD-3-Clause License, with the complete LANL copyright notice, government rights statement, license conditions, and disclaimer provided in the included LICENSE file. Third-party datasets retain their applicable rights and licensing terms, which are not superseded by the software license.

title: Forward Flux Sampling tropical cyclogenesis rates for the 2022 Atlantic season: simulation output
display_name: Forward Flux Sampling tropical cyclogenesis rates for the 2022 Atlantic season: simulation output
abstract: Forward Flux Sampling (FFS) output for "Conditional tropical cyclogenesis rates via rare-event sampling in a neural weather emulator" (Schreck, Chapman, Becker, Gagne). Model: SDL-WXFormer (1 degree, 6-hour steps), 98 ERA5 initial conditions (ICs) at 00 and 12 UTC from 21 August to 8 October 2022. State A: minimum MSLP above 1008 hPa. State B: minimum MSLP at or below 975 hPa with a warm core inside 10-40N, 100-20W. Interfaces (hPa): lambda0=1000.0, lambda1=987.2, lambda2=984.7, lambda3=981.2, lambda4=B=975.0. Files ffs_rate_statistics_98ICs.csv One row per IC: flux-phase counts and flux rate Phi_A0, direct-sampling state-B arrivals and rate k_direct, per-interface attempts/successes/failures/extratropical rejections and conditional crossing probabilities P1-P4 (lambda{i}_P_forward), FFS genesis rate k_FFS (ffs_rate_per_day), and cost/speedup estimates. ifs_ensemble_rates_98ICs.csv Same 98 ICs from the 50-member ECMWF IFS ensemble (WeatherBench2, 1.5 degree): lambda0 crossings, members crossing each interface, state-B arrivals, and rates. reactive_pathways/<IC>_reactive_pathways.json, <IC>_summary.txt Reactive pathway (lambda0 to state B) genealogies per IC: branch points, cluster weights, and per-pathway interface crossings with positions and MSLP. shot_outcomes_all_ICs.csv.gz One row per shooting attempt (2.3 million): IC, interface, parent and child configuration, outcome (success, returned_A, outside_geographic_bounds, extratropical), number of 6-hour steps, final and minimum MSLP, and CPS values at rejection. Used for the termination accounting in Methods and Supplementary Note 5. Code: https://github.com/NCAR/miles-tails

title: ReSource Tracker: Flowlines and Supplemental DMR Data for Colorado
display_name: ReSource Tracker: Flowlines and Supplemental DMR Data for Colorado
abstract: This dataset contains discharge monitoring report (DMR) data and a stream flowlines geopackage, prepared as input for ReSource Tracker, an open-source visualization tool for exploring wastewater discharges in surface waters. The data is not new observational data. It is a processed subset of publicly available from the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) and the United States Geographical Survey (USGS) Source Data Colorado municipal wastewater treatment plants were identified using the USEPA’s Integrated Compliance Information System – National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (ICIS-NPDES) database from the Enforcement and Compliance History Online (ECHO) Data Downloads page. Discharge Monitoring Report (DMR) data for wastewater treatment plant outfalls were collected from the USEPA’s ECHO dataset for the years 2019-2024 and retrieved in 2025. The NPDES database can be accessed at: https://echo.epa.gov/tools/data-downloads. The dataset includes polyline geometries, unique segment identifier (COMID), total upstream drainage area, upstream-downstream connectivity, and modeled mean annual and monthly streamflow. The attached file contains a Colorado-only subset of this data. The original data from USGS can be accessed at: https://www.usgs.gov/national-hydrography/nhdplus-high-resolution Files Flowlines_Colorado_Filtered.gpkg: Geopackage containing streamflow polylines for Colorado. This file is loaded directly for use in Resource Tracker CO_DMR_2019-2024_ResourceTracker.zip: Zip file containing 6 CSV files of DMR data, used as preprocessing. These data can be updated to included future DMR reports if users want to extend the dataset. Usage ReSource Tracker downloads the geopackage from this record automatically during installation. title: Data from: The temperature dependence of the pathogenic bacterial adhesin complex SdrG:Fgβ under sustained loads: a high-force slip bond
display_name: Data from: The temperature dependence of the pathogenic bacterial adhesin complex SdrG:Fgβ under sustained loads: a high-force slip bond
abstract: Staphylococcus epidermidis is the leading cause of medical-implant related infections. This pathogen attaches to medical implants coated in host fibrinogen via adhesin proteins. To resist high shear forces, adhesin-ligand rupture forces can exceed 2000 pN, a force that is much higher than streptavidin-biotin (150–300 pN). Yet, these adhesin-ligand complexes have a quite moderate KD (~380 nM). This nanomechanics is explained, in part, by catch-bond behavior where adhesin-ligand lifetimes increase with force. Notably, prior reports of adhesin catch-bond mechanics at both low (3–30 pN) and high (1100–1400 pN) forces have lifetimes that are difficult to reconcile. Here, we combined constant-velocity and constant-force assays and thereby showed slip-bond behavior over six decades of lifetimes first for SdrG:Fgβ (1000–2400 pN) and then for SdrE:CFH (800–2200 pN) from Staphylococcus aureus. Individual lifetimes for SdrE:CFH exceeded 15 min at 800 pN. To investigate the thermodynamics of SdrG:Fgβ stability, we measured its lifetime using the constant-force assay as a function of both force (1000–1800 pN) and temperature (10–37 °C). Analysis yielded the enthalpic-dissociation barrier (ΔH‡ = 40 ± 4 kBT) and, assuming an enthalpy-dominated barrier, the dissociation attempt frequency (~6×1010 s-‍1). Our results unambiguously demonstrate high-force slip-bond behavior for two different adhesin-ligand pairs and provide biophysical parameters governing the stability of key virulence factors.

title: Segmented projection image translation for large-area, high-resolution vat photopolymerization
display_name: Segmented projection image translation for large-area, high-resolution vat photopolymerization
abstract: High-resolution projection-based vat photopolymerization (VP) 3D printing enables rapid fabrication of highly detailed polymeric structures. However, expanding the build area traditionally compromises resolution, creating a fundamental trade-off between projected pixel size and printable area due to fixed digital micromirror device (DMD) pixel counts. Herein, we introduce Segmented Projection Image traNslation (SPIN), a simple implementation strategy that expands the effective projection area by applying controlled orbital translation to an off-axis objective lens within the optical infinity space. In this work, we demonstrate a projection-based VP printer implemented with SPIN that expands the effective build area by 4.8-fold, from a native 60.4 mm2 field to an expanded 290.5 mm2 domain. The SPIN-enabled printer produces isolated line features as thin as 9.8 ± 2.2 µm and fabricates intricate 3D truss structures with features as small as 30 µm. These results validate a practical route for extending microscale projection-based VP printing to larger build areas while preserving feature fidelity across stitched exposure fields.

title: Derived snow-cover duration, snowfall-event, and aerosol radiative forcing fields for High Mountain Asia, 2000–2020
display_name: Derived snow-cover duration, snowfall-event, and aerosol radiative forcing fields for High Mountain Asia, 2000–2020
abstract: Derived data fields underlying the figures and tables of Zargar et al., “Increasing Pre-monsoon Snowfall Darkens Himalayan Snowpack” (submitted to Geophysical Research Letters). The archive contains pre-monsoon (March–June) snow-cover duration climatology and trends, snowfall-event-day frequency and intensity distributions, cumulative aerosol-induced albedo darkening, and surface radiative forcing and melt potential across the Hindu Kush, Karakoram, Western Himalaya, Pamir and Western Kunlun, 2000–2020. Fields are derived from the NASA NSIDC STC MODSCAG/MODDRFS product together with ERA5, GPM IMERG, IMDAA, HAR v2, CMIP6 (CNRM-CM6-1) and MERRA-2. Each file is named for the figure or table it supports; see README.md for variable names, units, grid definition and provenance. Analysis code is archived separately.
source_display_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Data and software for "Spectral Analysis of Lunar Topography in the Artemis Landing Regions"
display_name: Data and software for "Spectral Analysis of Lunar Topography in the Artemis Landing Regions"
abstract: Software for mapping "elephant hide" texture in lunar digital elevation models, as described in "Spectral Analysis of Lunar Topography in the Artemis Landing Regions," which is accepted to The Planetary Science Journal. Output maps and scripts to produce all figures in the manuscript are included in this repository. quasiFFT.py Main software for EHT mapping/characterization funcs.py Helper functions for mapping and plotting loaders.py Helper functions to load DEMs params.py Constants used in analysis and plotting example.py Script to produce Figure 1 methods.py Script to produce Figure 2 ft_example.py Script to produce Figures 3, 4, and 5 results_map.py Script to produce Figures 6, 8, and 9 alignment_hist.py Script to produce Figure 7 results_1d.py Script to produce Figures 10, 11, and 12 temperature.py Script to produce Figure 13 validation.py Script to produce Figure 14 dem_overview.py Script to produce Figures 15-26 A3**_results_64ppd.py Output of spectral analysis for each Artemis landing region. Maps of EHT orientation and scale at a resolution of 64 ppd (~474 m/pxl)

title: Shortening agent skills leaves LLM agent cost unchanged: run outcomes, token counts, cost accounting and skill versions (40 SkillsBench tasks)
display_name: Shortening agent skills leaves LLM agent cost unchanged: run outcomes, token counts, cost accounting and skill versions (40 SkillsBench tasks)
abstract: Data and reproduction materials for the paper "Shortening agent skills leaves LLM agent cost unchanged" (Xiaonan Xu and Wenjing Wu, arXiv:2607.03048). The package contains run outcomes, token counts and cost accounting for 1,200 agent runs on 40 SkillsBench tasks, the skill versions given to the agent, and a script that reproduces the tables of the paper. The data archive skill_cost_open_data_v1.zip is unchanged from version 1 of this record. abstract: Five regional terrain meshes of Europa and their radiative view-factor matrices, ready for the Planetary Thermophysical Model 3D (PTM3D). They are the inputs of PTM3D's Europa terrain configurations and of the PTM3D GUI's Europa terrain card: Agenor Linea, Cilix crater, Pwyll crater, the pits and chaos near Rhadamanthys Linea, and the ridged terrain near Yelland Linea. Source and credit. The meshes are triangulations of the five SOCET SET digital terrain models (DTMs) of Bland, Michael (2022), Europa DEMs and Orthoimages in Support of Bland et al. 2021 (Remote Sensing), figshare, doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.16904632.v1 (CC BY 4.0). Those DTMs were produced by Michael T. Bland and Donna M. Galuszka at the U.S. Geological Survey Astrogeology Science Center from images acquired by NASA's Galileo Solid State Imager (SSI), with funding from NASA PDART award NNH16AC37I, and support Bland, M. T., Kirk, R. L., Galuszka, D. M., Mayer, D. P., Beyer, R. A., and Fergason, R. L. (2021), How Well Do We Know Europa's Topography? An Evaluation of the Variability in Digital Terrain Models of Europa, Remote Sensing 13(24), 5097, doi:10.3390/rs13245097. Please cite the source dataset and that paper as well as this dataset. Usage note from the source. The source products "should only be used to assess and or verify the conclusions described in Bland et al. 2021 (published in Remote Sensing), as the DTMs themselves have been superseded by updated versions that are registered to Europa's cartographic coordinate system." PTM3D uses the relief; treat results from these meshes as studies of terrains of that character, not of mapped locations. Changes from the source. Each DTM was triangulated at full resolution with PTM3D's dtm_to_ply_delaunay --body-radius 1562090 (the rasters' own sphere), and each mesh's view-factor matrix was computed with the PTM3D engine's sparse view-factor builder; PTM3D v1.1.1 rebuilds all five matrices byte-identically. DATASET_README.md and PROVENANCE.json (inside the archive; the README is also attached separately) record every step, checksum and parameter. Use. In a PTM3D checkout: python3 scripts/fetch_data.py --dataset europa-terrain, which verifies the archive's SHA-256 and unpacks it into data/external/sutton_DEMs/.

The daily file (airnow_daily_classified_US.csv.gz) comprises 3,754,468 monitor-days at 1,732 monitors; monitor locations are in airnow_pm25_location_us_attrs.zip, joined by AQSID; and the pipeline code is release v1.0.2 of https://github.com/mingonchung/multihazard_pm25_pipeline. title: iButton and Tinytag snow temperature measurements at Teller 27 and Kougarok 64 from 2023-2024, Seward Peninsula, Alaska
display_name: iButton and Tinytag snow temperature measurements at Teller 27 and Kougarok 64 from 2023-2024, Seward Peninsula, Alaska
abstract: Snow temperature measurements were collected at the NGEE Arctic Teller Road Site at mile marker 27 (TL_MM27) and at the Kougarok Road Site at mile marker 64 (KG_MM64) on the Seward Peninsula. Data were collected using iButton DS1921G-F5# Thermochron miniature temperature sensors (https://www.ibuttonlink.com/products/ds1921g) and Tinytag TGP-4017 internal sensors (https://www.micronmeters.com/product/tgp-4017-internal-sensor-40-to-85-c-40-f-to-185-f) deployed across the Teller 27 and Kougarok 64 sites. These sensors are a cost-efficient way to collect snowpack temperatures at a higher spatial resolution than what is normally achieved. iButton data were collected every 4 hours beginning on October 1 2023 to September 6, 2024. Tinytag data were collected every 30 minutes from October 1, 2023 to September 11, 2024. In total, data were collected from 166 iButtons and 28 Tinytags. This dataset contains four *.csv files of near-ground surface temperatures at various locations throughout each study site, one compiled *.csv data file of all sensors and sites, and one *.kml file of sensor locations. Data were collected throughout the snow cover season so that snowpack characteristics could be derived using the temperature data. Sensors were placed both under and on top of vegetation to better capture the spatial variability of snow properties across each domain. The Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments: Arctic (NGEE Arctic) is a research effort to reduce uncertainty in Earth System Models by developing a predictive understanding of carbon-rich Arctic ecosystems and feedbacks to climate. NGEE Arctic was supported by the Department of Energy’s Office of Biological and Environmental Research. The NGEE Arctic project had two field research sites: 1) located within the Arctic polygonal tundra coastal region on the Barrow Environmental Observatory (BEO) and the North Slope near Utqiagvik (Barrow), Alaska and 2) multiple areas on the discontinuous permafrost region of the Seward Peninsula north of Nome, Alaska. Through observations, experiments, and synthesis with existing datasets, NGEE Arctic provided an enhanced knowledge base for multi-scale modeling and contributed to improved process representation at global pan-Arctic scales within the Department of Energy’s Earth system Model (the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, or E3SM), and specifically within the E3SM Land Model component (ELM).

title: Near-infrared spectroscopy predictions of forage nitrogen, crude protein, and fiber for plant, lichen, and moss specimens across land-cover types in the Sattasniemi reindeer herding district, northern Finland, summer 2025
display_name: Near-infrared spectroscopy predictions of forage nitrogen, crude protein, and fiber for plant, lichen, and moss specimens across land-cover types in the Sattasniemi reindeer herding district, northern Finland, summer 2025
abstract: The ranging patterns of semi-domesticated reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) are shaped in part by their nutritional landscape - the spatially explicit distribution of forage quality across the environment. Characterizing that landscape requires moving beyond coarse land-cover classifications to resolve nutritional variation among plant functional types and vegetation communities. This dataset accompanies a study in the Sattasniemi reindeer herding district of northern Finland (Finnish Lapland) that links land-cover type, plant functional type, and forage nutritional composition. Working through knowledge co-production with local reindeer herders, we identified nine land-cover types that together account for the great majority of the district and sampled vegetation across 72 field sites during the summer (July) of 2025. Individual leaves (and whole thalli for lichens) were dried and scanned with a field-deployable near-infrared reflectance spectrometer (NIRS, 350-2500 nm [nanometers]). For each scan we predicted nitrogen, crude protein (nitrogen x 6.25), neutral detergent fiber (NDF), and acid detergent fiber (ADF) using calibrations developed against wet-chemistry reference values from the combined Norwegian and Finnish 2025 collections. This file contains the resulting replicate-level NIRS predictions for each specimen, together with its taxon, plant functional type, land-cover type, site, site pair, plant part, and collection date. In the associated study, forested peatlands and mires supported the highest crude protein and only moderate fiber, and herder-reported summer habitat use tracked cover-weighted forage protein. The data demonstrate that field-deployable NIRS can characterize forage chemistry across many taxa and habitats at spatial, temporal, and taxonomic resolutions that conventional wet chemistry cannot practically match, providing foundational data for understanding reindeer ranging decisions and informing reindeer husbandry. Predictions for organisms outside the calibration domain (bryophytes, lichens (ADF, NDF), and fungi) are extrapolations and should be interpreted with caution.
